documents.title: Guidelines for AI Use at The City College of New York
documents.summary: Provost-posted interim guidelines for CCNY while schools draft their own AI policies. They stress disclosure of AI use, data privacy with CoPilot as default tool, explicit syllabus statements, in-class assessment instead of detectors, and AI training for students.
documents.stance_why: The guidelines call themselves "not policy" and require each instructor to put "your own guidelines for the acceptable use of AI tools" in the syllabus, saying the line "is likely to be different in different classes". No default ban or permission is set, so delegates.

units.why: The document disclaims being policy: "which are not policy but contain some advice". This sets the status and scope of the whole text, so it is P56 (institution-level framework/preamble), informs, general; it sets no rule itself.
units.anchor: which are not policy but contain some advice

units.why: Divisions and Schools "have been charged with drafting their own AI policies", so the college pushes the actual rule-setting down to units. P04 (rule set by each unit/instructor) fits better than P54 because it assigns who decides rather than promising review.
units.anchor: have been charged with drafting their own AI policies
units.policy: Each Division and School of the College is charged with drafting its own AI policy.

units.why: The principles say AI "can be powerful tools for problem solving" when used properly but "can interfere with the primary mission" when not. It is a statement of purpose and principle, so P56, informs.
units.anchor: When used inappropriately they can interfere with the primary mission of the College
units.policy: AI used properly and appropriately can be a powerful tool for problem solving; used inappropriately it can interfere with the College's primary mission of educating students.

units.why: The document says research and creative work are not addressed "other than to say that its use should always be declared". This is a rule on research use, so P62, with should modality because of "should always be declared".
units.anchor: its use should always be declared
units.frag_start: It is not a document that
units.policy: AI use in research and creative work should always be declared.

units.why: "many of the platforms utilize user input as training data" is a privacy fact that motivates later rules. It is P50 (protect data), informs.
units.anchor: many of the platforms utilize user input as training data
units.policy: Many AI platforms use user input as training data, so users should be aware of privacy and data security concerns.

units.why: "strongly recommended that CoPilot be your default AI tool" with CUNY login steers users to the university-licensed tool. P50 ("prefer university-vetted or licensed tools") fits; P17 is about a course-provided tool and does not fit as well.
units.anchor: strongly recommended that CoPilot be your default AI tool
units.policy: Microsoft CoPilot used through Microsoft 365 with a CUNY login is strongly recommended as the default AI tool.

units.why: Non-public institutional data and "FERPA-protected data, should not be uploaded to any platform other than CoPilot". A data-protection rule, P50, should-not.
units.anchor: FERPA-protected data, should not be uploaded to any platform other than CoPilot
units.policy: Institutional data that is not publicly available, and especially FERPA-protected data, should not be uploaded to any platform other than CoPilot.

units.why: "CUNY's policy on data in the Cloud must be followed" binds anyone uploading data to LLMs. Data protection, P50, must.
units.anchor: on data in the Cloud must be followed
units.policy: CUNY's policy on data in the Cloud must be followed when uploading data to LLMs.

units.why: AI-like spelling and grammar correction "need not be declared". This is a rule specific to prose editing, so P18, with may modality; it also relaxes disclosure but P18 is the better home.
units.anchor: such use need not be declared
units.frag_start: While the tools have become more
units.policy: AI-like tools used for correcting spelling, punctuation and simple grammatical errors need not be declared.

units.why: "You may decide otherwise in a class where spelling, punctuation and/or grammar are core parts" lets instructors change the exemption per class, so P04.
units.anchor: You may decide otherwise in a class where spelling, punctuation and/or grammar
units.policy: Instructors may decide otherwise in a class where spelling, punctuation and/or grammar are core parts of the curriculum.

units.why: "any other use of AI tools in the creation of a document must be declared" is a disclosure requirement, P24, must.
units.anchor: any other use of AI tools in the creation of a document must be declared
units.frag_start: Apart from such cases, any other
units.policy: Any use of AI tools in the creation of a document, other than spelling, punctuation and simple grammar correction, must be declared.

units.why: "The declaration should include which AI tool was used and what content it created" specifies the content of the disclosure (tool and output), so P25 rather than P24.
units.anchor: The declaration should include which AI tool was used and what content it created

units.why: "when AI tools are used in decision making, their use must be disclosed". The actor is whoever makes decisions with AI (faculty/staff), not a student submission, so P47 rather than P24.
units.anchor: when AI tools are used in decision making, their use must be disclosed
units.frag_start: Similarly, when AI tools are used

units.why: "at minimum, what data, platform and prompts were used" specifies required details of the disclosure of AI in decisions. P25 (tool, prompt, output details).
units.anchor: what data, platform and prompts were used
units.policy: Disclosure of AI use in decision making should include, at minimum, what data, platform and prompts were used.

units.why: Most principles "apply to the use of AI tools by faculty in the classroom and by students in doing class assignments and exams". This sets scope of the principles across actors, so P56 (scope), informs.
units.anchor: principles apply to the use of AI tools by faculty in the classroom
units.policy: Most of the general principles apply to AI use by faculty in the classroom and by students in assignments and exams.

units.why: "it is essential that your syllabus include your own guidelines for the acceptable use of AI tools in your class" addresses instructors and is a syllabus-statement requirement, P09.
units.anchor: your syllabus include your own guidelines for the acceptable use of AI tools
units.policy: The syllabus must include the instructor's own guidelines for the acceptable use of AI tools in the class.

units.why: "Do not assume that students know where the line is... Be as explicit as possible" tells instructors to make expectations explicit. P09 (state expectations) rather than P10, which is about students asking.
units.anchor: Be as explicit as possible
units.policy: Instructors should not assume students know where the line between appropriate and inappropriate use is, and should be as explicit as possible.

units.why: "the line between appropriate and inappropriate use is likely to be different in different classes" says each class sets its own line; P11 fits because it is about rules not carrying across courses.
units.anchor: the line between appropriate and inappropriate use is likely to be different in different classes
units.frag_start: and be clear that the line
units.policy: Instructors should be clear that the line between appropriate and inappropriate AI use is likely to be different in different classes.

units.why: "Possible sanctions for inappropriate use should also be included" in the syllabus; this asks for penalties to be stated in advance, P37.
units.anchor: Possible sanctions for inappropriate use should also be included
units.policy: The syllabus should include possible sanctions for inappropriate AI use.

units.why: "Remind the students of these guidelines on a regular basis" is about communicating expectations repeatedly, so P09 (communicate expectations) is the nearest type.
units.anchor: Remind the students of these guidelines on a regular basis
units.policy: Instructors remind students of the AI guidelines on a regular basis.

units.why: "it is incumbent upon us as a college to provide training in the use of AI" justifies AI skill-building by the workforce, so P44, encourage.
units.anchor: incumbent upon us as a college to provide training in the use of AI
units.frag_start: Given that our students will be
units.policy: Because students will enter a workforce using AI tools, the college is obliged to provide training in the use of AI.

units.why: "Faculty should therefore consider including artificial intelligence tools in their courses, as appropriate" recommends teaching with AI. P44 (courses teach AI use) fits better than P02 since it is not a default student rule.
units.anchor: consider including artificial intelligence tools in their courses
units.policy: Faculty should consider including artificial intelligence tools in their courses, as appropriate.

units.why: "The level of engagement with AI and the specific tools used, will naturally vary from one major to another" leaves engagement to each field, so P04.
units.anchor: The level of engagement with AI and the specific tools used, will naturally vary
units.policy: The level of engagement with AI and the specific tools used vary from one major to another.

units.why: "in addition to the College's and CUNY's Academic Integrity Policy, not in place of them" and students should be reminded. It ties AI rules to integrity rules, so P36.
units.anchor: in addition to the College’s and CUNY’s Academic Integrity Policy, not in place of them
units.frag_start: Guidelines around the use of AI
units.policy: Guidelines around the use of AI tools are in addition to the College's and CUNY's Academic Integrity Policy, not in place of them; students should be reminded.

units.why: Violations that "rise to the level of violations of academic integrity, should be reported to the College's Academic Integrity Officer". An integrity-process routing rule, P36.
units.anchor: should be reported to the College’s Academic Integrity Officer
units.policy: Violations of an instructor's AI policy that rise to the level of academic integrity violations should be reported to the College's Academic Integrity Officer and are handled through that office.

units.why: "Automatic AI detection systems are not reliable" is a direct statement against relying on detectors, P39.
units.anchor: Automatic AI detection systems are not reliable
units.frag_end: AI-related academic integrity violations can be difficult
units.policy: Automatic AI detection systems are not reliable.

units.why: "It is worth reminding them why they are here and how AI misuse can defeat that purpose" frames misuse as undermining learning and long-term prospects, P41.
units.anchor: how AI misuse can defeat that purpose
units.frag_start: It is worth reminding them why
units.policy: Students are reminded how AI misuse can defeat the purpose of their education, giving perhaps short-term gain but long-term damage to their prospects.

units.why: "More effective measures... can come from pedagogical and operational changes" states that redesign works better than detection; P35 (redesign around AI), informs.
units.anchor: misuse of AI in coursework can come from pedagogical and operational changes
units.policy: More effective measures for preventing misuse of AI in coursework can come from pedagogical and operational changes.

units.why: "faculty should consider having assessments that are a significant part of the course grade done in person and in class" shifts weight to proctored work, P33.
units.anchor: assessments that are a significant part of the course grade done in person
units.policy: Faculty should consider having assessments that are a significant part of the course grade done in person and in class.

units.why: Courses with term papers "will need to revert to shorter in-class work and may need to schedule an in-class final exam". Course-structure redesign, P35 (P33 is the general weight shift stated just before).
units.anchor: will need to revert to shorter in-class work
units.frag_end: previously the final was a take-home assignment
units.policy: Classes that previously used term papers as a major component may need to revert to shorter in-class work and schedule an in-class final exam instead of a take-home final.

units.why: "faculty should also consider collecting cell phones prior to in-class exams" is a device rule for exams, P22.
units.anchor: collecting cell phones prior to in-class exams
units.frag_end: rightful owners when the exam is done
units.policy: Faculty should consider collecting cell phones prior to in-class exams, provided they can efficiently return them afterward.

units.why: "very clearly, and in writing, state what AI use is allowed and not allowed in your class" is the closing requirement to put the rule in writing, P09.
units.anchor: very clearly, and in writing, state what AI use is allowed and not allowed
units.frag_start: just be sure to very clearly,
units.policy: Instructors must state clearly, in writing, what AI use is allowed and not allowed in their class.

units.why: "A few sample AI policy statements, appropriate for use on syllabi, are provided" in the Graduate Center guidelines; pointing faculty to resources is P63.
units.anchor: A few sample AI policy statements, appropriate for use on syllabi
units.frag_start: A few sample AI policy statements,
units.policy: Sample AI policy statements appropriate for syllabi are provided toward the end of the Graduate Center guidelines.

units.why: "Faculty my also wish to consult the thoughtful guidelines posted by the Graduate Center" points faculty to outside guidance, P63.
units.anchor: wish to consult the thoughtful guidelines posted by the Graduate Center
units.policy: Faculty may wish to consult the guidelines posted by the Graduate Center.

documents.title: CUNY Academic Integrity Policy (2024)
documents.summary: CUNY system-wide integrity policy revised in 2024 to cover AI. AI appears in the definitions of cheating and plagiarism (unauthorized generation, uncited AI content, exam devices), in the substantial-violation example, and in the explanation stressing responsible AI use.
documents.stance_why: The policy defines "unauthorized use" of AI systems and generating content "without written authorization from the instructor" as cheating, so AI is banned unless authorized, while instructors set the usage policy per assignment. That is restrict.

units.why: The cheating definition covers "unauthorized use... of... artificial intelligence (AI) systems" during an academic exercise, classing unauthorized AI use as misconduct: P36.
units.anchor: devices, artificial intelligence (AI) systems, or communication during an academic exercise
units.policy: Cheating is the unauthorized use or attempted use of material, information, notes, study aids, devices, artificial intelligence (AI) systems, or communication during an academic exercise.

units.why: "Copying from another person or from a generative AI system" is listed as cheating. It bans having AI produce submitted work, P19.
units.anchor: Copying from another person or from a generative AI system
units.frag_end: allowing others to copy work submitted for credit or a grade
units.policy: Copying from a generative AI system is cheating.

units.why: Submitting class assignments or exams to third-party platforms beyond those assigned, without professor authorization, is cheating. It restricts uploading course work to outside tools, so P49.
units.anchor: submitting class assignments or exams to third party platforms and websites
units.policy: Uploading work or submitting class assignments or exams to third party platforms and websites beyond those assigned for the class is cheating without the professor's authorization.

units.why: "Any use of generative AI tools must be in line with the usage policy for specific assignments as defined in the syllabus" makes the course or assignment the source of the rule, P04.
units.anchor: must be in line with the usage policy for specific assignments
units.frag_start: Any use of generative AI tools
units.policy: Any use of generative AI tools must be in line with the usage policy for specific assignments as defined in the course syllabus and/or communicated by the instructor.

units.why: Using AI to generate content "without written authorization from the instructor" is cheating, so AI is banned unless the instructor permits in writing. P06 (default ban unless authorized) fits better than P19 because the authorization condition is the key content.
units.anchor: without written authorization from the instructor
units.frag_start: Using artificial intelligence tools to generate content
units.frag_end: without written authorization from the instructor
units.policy: Using AI tools, including language models or code generators, to generate content for assignments or exams without written authorization from the instructor is cheating.

units.why: Submitting AI-generated content as "solely your own work" is cheating. This is ownership of submitted work, P29.
units.anchor: Submitting content generated by another person or an AI tool
units.policy: Submitting content generated by an AI tool as solely your own work is cheating, including content generated or altered by AI or digital paraphrasing tools without proper citation.

units.why: "without proper citation" makes citing AI-altered content the condition for acceptability, i.e. an attribution requirement, P24.
units.anchor: content generated or altered by AI or digital paraphrasing tools without proper citation
units.policy: Content generated or altered by AI or digital paraphrasing tools must be properly cited.

units.why: Using electronic devices during an examination "to copy, retrieve, generate or send information" without authorization is cheating. Exam rule, P22.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use during an examination of notes, prepared answers, or any electronic devices
units.policy: Unauthorized use during an examination of notes, prepared answers, or any electronic devices to copy, retrieve, generate or send information is cheating.

units.why: Plagiarism includes "Copying... an AI tool's actual words or images without the use of quotation marks and citations", an attribution rule for AI text, P24.
units.anchor: an AI tool’s actual words or images without the use of quotation marks and citations
units.policy: Copying an AI tool's actual words or images without quotation marks and citations attributing them to their source is plagiarism.

units.why: Plagiarism includes "use of AI-generated content... even when paraphrased, without citing the AI as the source". It extends the citation rule to paraphrase, P24.
units.anchor: even when paraphrased, without citing the AI as the source
units.frag_end: citing the AI as the source
units.policy: Using AI-generated content, in whole or in part, even when paraphrased, without citing the AI as the source is plagiarism.

units.why: "Each college shall subscribe to an electronic plagiarism detection service" is a similarity-checking mandate, P40; it does not mention AI detection by name, so the AI relevance is general.
units.anchor: Each college shall subscribe to an electronic plagiarism detection service
units.frag_end: available for use by the faculty
units.policy: Each college shall subscribe to an electronic plagiarism detection service and notify students that it is available for faculty use.

units.why: A faculty member who suspects a violation "shall review with the student the facts and circumstances... whenever feasible" before reporting, P57.
units.anchor: shall review with the student the facts and circumstances of the suspected violation whenever feasible
units.frag_start: A faculty member who suspects that
units.policy: A faculty member who suspects a violation shall review with the student the facts and circumstances of the suspected violation whenever feasible.

units.why: "generating entire assignments or exam responses using AI without authorization" is named an example of a substantial violation that justifies disciplinary sanctions. A penalty-severity statement, P37.
units.anchor: generating entire assignments or exam responses using AI without authorization
units.policy: Generating entire assignments or exam responses using AI without authorization is an example of a substantial violation for which disciplinary sanctions may be sought.

units.why: A student who denies dishonesty gets "written notice of the charges", "the right to appear" and to present witnesses. It guarantees a right to respond in integrity cases (including AI cases), P64.
units.anchor: the right to appear before the Committee
units.frag_start: In a case where a student denies
units.policy: Students who deny academic dishonesty are provided written notice of the charges, the right to appear before the Committee and the right to present witness statements and/or call witnesses.

units.why: The explanation says policy was revised because "the current policy does not address the advent of Artificial Intelligence", which explains why the policy changed over time: P54.
units.anchor: the current policy does not address the advent of Artificial Intelligence
units.policy: The 2022 Academic Integrity Policy was revised because it did not address the advent of Artificial Intelligence and its use by students at CUNY.

units.why: "Preparing students to learn from and use AI responsibly and ethically is critical to the University's mission" states the purpose of preparing students to use AI, P44.
units.anchor: Preparing students to learn from and use AI responsibly and ethically is critical
units.frag_end: rigor of the University’s academic programs
units.policy: Preparing students to learn from and use AI responsibly and ethically is critical to the University's mission, academic integrity and the rigor of its programs.

units.why: "students must become facile with the use of AI to learn effectively... and to prepare for their AI-assisted careers" is a career-preparation rationale, P44.
units.anchor: students must become facile with the use of AI to learn effectively in today’s world
units.frag_end: careers and lives in the future
units.policy: Students must become facile with the use of AI to learn effectively and to prepare for their AI-assisted careers and lives.

notes: No school or computing-unit policy found (per collect file). Document 1 text has a typo ('Faculty my'). Document 2 rules are general integrity rules; only AI-related passages were coded, plus a few generic procedure rules (plagiarism service, review with student, hearing rights) that apply to AI cases.
